passage:
In the kasba of Palanpur, Sudha had worked beside Tanvir at his family's cloth shop all summer before college reopened. On Tuesday, in front of two customers, he snapped, "Can't you do anything right? Even a child can fold a saree." She kept folding, cheeks burning.
On Thursday he walked in smiling and put a box on the counter: a new phone, far better than her cracked one. "For you. Hardworking people deserve good things."
Sudha looked at the box. It felt like he was trying to fold Tuesday away and put it on a high shelf. She pushed it gently back. "Tanvir, thank you, but I can't take this. What I'd like is for us to talk about what you said on Tuesday."
His smile slipped. "It was nothing."
"It wasn't nothing to me," she said.

qa.q: What did Tanvir say to Sudha on Tuesday?
qa.a: "Can't you do anything right? Even a child can fold a saree."

qa.q: Why did the new phone feel wrong to Sudha?
qa.a: It seemed like an attempt to put Tuesday's insult away without talking about it, so accepting it would feel like agreeing the hurt didn't matter.

qa.q: What choice did Sudha make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: She returned the gift kindly and asked to talk about Tuesday, which keeps the relationship open while making clear that words matter more than presents. 👍

qa.q: What might Tanvir be feeling when his smile slips?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and uneasy, since the gift was his way to avoid admitting what he said, and now he has to face it.

grounding: A young woman insulted in front of customers is handed an expensive phone with a smile, and kindly says she would rather talk about what was said.

passage:
In their shared flat in Berlin, Felix had mocked Aiko's accent at a party, loudly, doing an impression while his friends laughed. Aiko left early.
The next evening Felix knocked on her door holding a bag from an expensive bookshop: a beautiful illustrated edition of the novel she had been saving up for. "Peace offering!" he said, with his brightest grin.
Aiko held the heavy book. It was exactly what she wanted, which somehow made it worse. It felt like the party was being wrapped in expensive paper and put away. "Felix," she said, "this is really generous. But I'd rather hear what you think about last night."
Felix shifted from foot to foot. "I mean, it was a joke..."
"It didn't feel like one," Aiko said. "Can we talk about it? The book can wait."

qa.q: What did Felix give Aiko?
qa.a: An illustrated edition of the novel she had been saving up for.

qa.q: Why did the perfect gift somehow make things feel worse for Aiko?
qa.a: It felt as if the hurtful impression was being wrapped up and put away without being talked about, as though her hurt didn't need words.

qa.q: What choice did Aiko make, and why might it help?
qa.a: She thanked Felix but asked to talk about the party first, making clear in a kind way that the conversation mattered more than the book.

qa.q: Why might Felix have chosen an expensive gift instead of an apology?
qa.a: He may feel guilty but awkward about admitting the impression was hurtful, and a gift felt easier than saying he was wrong.

grounding: A student in Berlin mocked at a party receives an expensive book as a 'peace offering' and gently says she would rather talk about what happened.

"The stupidest thing I've heard all year." That was what Raghav had called Vidya's idea in the college chemistry lab, in front of the whole project group. Vidya said nothing and packed up early.
Two days later a courier arrived at the lab bench: a box of expensive imported chocolates and a card in Raghav's handwriting, "For the best lab partner!" He was grinning across the room, waiting for her to open it. The other students cooed. Vidya felt her chest tighten. Everyone was acting as if everything was fine now.
After the practical, she caught Raghav by the fume hood. "Thanks for the chocolates," she said quietly. "But what I'd really like is an apology for what you said in front of the group. The chocolates don't do that."
Raghav's grin faded. He looked at the floor for a long moment.

qa.q: What did the card with the chocolates say?
qa.a: "For the best lab partner!"

qa.q: Why did Vidya's chest tighten when the other students cooed?
qa.a: She felt the insult was being wiped away in public, as if everyone had decided it was fine without her ever being heard.

qa.q: Which choice of Vidya's was wise, and why?
qa.a: Speaking to Raghav privately, thanking him but asking for an actual apology, which was kind but clear that talking matters more than gifts.

qa.q: What might Raghav be feeling as he looks at the floor?
qa.a: Embarrassed and perhaps ashamed, realising the chocolates couldn't cover what he said in front of the group.

grounding: A student publicly insulted by her lab partner receives expensive chocolates instead of an apology, and privately asks for the apology.

passage:
Dear Kunal,
Thank you for the headphones. They're lovely, and I know they cost a lot. That's actually why I'm writing instead of just saying thanks.
At the drama club reading on Friday, in front of everyone, you called my script "sentimental rubbish for aunties". People laughed. I went home and didn't sleep much. Then on Monday the box appeared on my desk, and you smiled at me as if the whole thing was settled.
It felt like the headphones were meant to wipe Friday away. I don't think they can. I'm not angry with you, not really. I just want us to talk about what you said, whether you meant it, and why it came out that way.
Could we get chai after rehearsal on Thursday? I'd honestly rather have that than any gift.
Bhavna

qa.q: What did Kunal call Bhavna's script at the drama club reading?
qa.a: "Sentimental rubbish for aunties."

qa.q: How did the headphones make Bhavna feel, and why?
qa.a: Uneasy rather than pleased, because they seemed meant to wipe Friday away without Kunal ever speaking about the insult.

qa.q: What is wise about the way Bhavna responds?
qa.a: Bhavna thanks Kunal kindly, explains that a gift can't erase the hurt, and asks for a chai conversation, keeping the door open without pretending it's fine.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel reading that Bhavna would rather talk than have any gift?
qa.a: Kunal may feel embarrassed at first, but also relieved to be offered a real way to mend things instead of hoping a present would do it.

grounding: Shows a student who was insulted and then given an expensive gift feeling the hurt is being wiped away, and kindly asking to talk instead.

passage:
Rubina, look at this. Perfume. The real kind, in a glass box. Deepika left it on my bed this morning with a note that just said "For my favourite!" and a heart.
You were there last night. At her birthday dinner, when I said I'd never tried sushi, she laughed and told the whole table, "Trisha's straight from the village, she thinks wasabi is chutney." Everyone laughed. I laughed too, then went to the bathroom and stood there for ten minutes.
And now this. This morning in the corridor she smiled at me so brightly, like it never happened. Like the box closes the matter.
I'm not throwing it away. I'm not angry enough for that. But at lunch I told her, nicely, "Thank you for the perfume. What I'd really like is to talk about last night." She went quiet. We're having tea at five.
Is that strange? I'd trade the box for one proper sorry.

qa.q: What did Deepika's note with the perfume say?
qa.a: "For my favourite!", with a heart.

qa.q: Why did the bright smile in the corridor bother Trisha?
qa.a: It felt as if Deepika was treating the perfume as closing the matter, wiping away the hurtful joke without ever talking about it.

qa.q: What did Trisha get right in the words chosen at lunch?
qa.a: Thanking Deepika for the perfume but kindly asking to talk about last night, which is honest about the hurt without starting a fight.

qa.q: Why might Deepika have chosen perfume instead of an apology?
qa.a: Deepika may have felt guilty but found a gift easier than admitting the joke was hurtful, hoping it would smooth things over quietly.

grounding: Illustrates a young woman mocked at a dinner who receives an expensive present and a bright smile, feels the hurt is being erased, and gently asks to talk.
